lessons.title: Lesson 1: The road map: what a California nonprofit needs
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the main setup filings in the right order and the office that handles each one.
This lesson builds toward: Given the steps to start a California charity, you will list the main setup filings in order and the office that handles each one, with every filing in the right order.
In California, a charity usually becomes a nonprofit public benefit corporation. Being a nonprofit corporation is a state matter. Being tax-exempt is a separate step: once with the IRS (federal) and once with the Franchise Tax Board (state). Fundraising charities also register with the Attorney General.
The usual order is: 1) choose your purpose, name and first board; 2) file articles of incorporation with the Secretary of State; 3) get an EIN from the IRS; 4) adopt bylaws and hold the first board meeting; 5) file the Statement of Information; 6) apply for federal 501(c)(3) status; 7) apply for California exemption with the Franchise Tax Board; 8) register with the Attorney General's Registry of Charities.
Doing these in order matters. For example, the IRS tells corporations to register with the state before applying for an EIN, and the Attorney General asks for your articles and bylaws when you register.
Step by step:
- Write your mission in one or two sentences.
- Pick three or more people for your first board, if you can.
- Write the eight steps in order on one page.
- Next to each step, write the office: Secretary of State, IRS, Franchise Tax Board or Attorney General.
Words to know:
- Nonprofit public benefit corporation: the California type of corporation most charities use; it serves the public, not owners.
- 501(c)(3): the section of the federal tax code for charities; donations to them can usually be tax-deductible.
- Tax-exempt: not required to pay income tax, after an agency approves it.
Official sources:
- California Secretary of State: Corporations - California (Domestic) forms and fees
- IRS: Get an Employer Identification Number
- California Franchise Tax Board: Charities and nonprofits (Form 3500 / 3500A)
- California Attorney General: Registry of Charities, initial registration (CT-1)
Try it now: Write your nonprofit's mission in one or two sentences. Then write the eight setup steps in order and the office for each one. Keep this page: it becomes your final setup plan.
You can now list the setup filings for a California nonprofit in order and name the office that handles each.

check.q: Which office handles California tax exemption?
check.why: Tax exemption is with the IRS (federal) and the Franchise Tax Board (state).

check.q: A founder wants to apply for an EIN before filing articles. What do you tell them?
options: File articles with the Secretary of State first, as the IRS tells corporations
Register with the Attorney General first
check.why: The IRS tells corporations to register with the state before applying for an EIN.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Filing articles of incorporation
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the right articles form and file it with the Secretary of State.
This lesson builds toward: Given your nonprofit's purpose, you will choose the right articles of incorporation form and plan the Statement of Information, with the filing place and due dates correct.
Articles of incorporation create your corporation. The California Secretary of State has three nonprofit versions: Form ARTS-PB (public benefit), Form ARTS-RE (religious) and Form ARTS-MU (mutual benefit). The filing fee shown for each was $30 when we checked.
Most charities use public benefit. A church or ministry may use the religious form. Mutual benefit is for groups that serve their own members, like some clubs, and does not fit most charities. If you plan to seek 501(c)(3) status, the IRS needs certain words in your articles about your purpose and what happens to your assets if you close. Read the form's instructions, and ask a nonprofit attorney or help center to look it over.
You can file online at bizfile Online (bizfileonline.sos.ca.gov), or by mail or in person. Search the name first to make sure it is free. Within 90 days, you also file a Statement of Information (Form SI-100, $20), and again every two years.
Step by step:
- Search your name on bizfile Online.
- Pick the form: ARTS-PB for most charities, ARTS-RE for religious groups.
- Fill it in with your name, purpose and agent for service of process.
- File online and pay the fee shown on the official page.
- Put the Statement of Information (SI-100) on your calendar: within 90 days, then every two years.
Words to know:
- Articles of incorporation: the short document that legally creates your corporation.
- Agent for service of process: the person or company that agrees to receive legal papers for the nonprofit.
- Statement of Information: a form that tells the state your address and officers; nonprofits file SI-100.
Official sources:
- California Secretary of State: Corporations - California (Domestic) forms and fees
- California Secretary of State: Statement of Information (SI-100 for nonprofits)
- California Secretary of State: bizfile Online
Try it now: Open the Secretary of State forms page. Find the articles form that fits your group and write down its form name and current fee. Then find the SI-100 fee and add both to your plan with a due date for the SI-100.
You can now choose the right articles form, find its fee on the official page, and schedule your Statement of Information.

check.q: Which articles form does not fit most charities?
check.why: Mutual benefit is for groups that serve their own members and does not fit most charities.

check.q: You want to name your nonprofit "Hope Kitchen." What do you do before filing?
options: Ask AI if the name is free
Pay a website to reserve it
Search the name first to make sure it is free
check.why: Search the name first to make sure it is free.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Getting your EIN, bylaws and first board meeting
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Get a free EIN safely and prepare the first board meeting.
This lesson builds toward: After your articles are filed, you will get a free EIN on irs.gov and plan the first board meeting, with private numbers typed only into the official IRS site and every first-meeting decision listed.
An EIN (Employer Identification Number) is the nonprofit's federal tax ID. You need it for a bank account, for payroll and for your tax-exemption applications. The IRS says you never have to pay for an EIN. Some websites charge for it: avoid them and apply on irs.gov.
The IRS online tool needs the responsible party's Social Security number or ITIN, and it must be finished in one sitting. Type these private numbers only into the official IRS site, never into an AI tool, an email or a random website. Print or save the confirmation letter.
Bylaws are your rules: how many directors, how they are elected, how meetings work, and who signs checks. At the first board meeting, the board adopts the bylaws, elects officers, approves opening a bank account and adopts a conflict-of-interest policy. Write minutes and keep them.
Step by step:
- Wait until the Secretary of State has filed your articles.
- Go to irs.gov and apply for the EIN with the free online tool.
- Save the EIN confirmation letter in your records folder.
- Draft bylaws and a conflict-of-interest policy.
- Hold the first board meeting and write the minutes.
Words to know:
- EIN: Employer Identification Number: the free federal tax ID for an organization.
- Bylaws: the written rules for how the nonprofit and its board run.
- Minutes: the written record of what the board decided at a meeting.
- Conflict-of-interest policy: rules for what a board member must do when a decision could benefit them personally.
Official sources:
- IRS: Get an Employer Identification Number
Try it now: Make a first-meeting agenda with five items: adopt bylaws, elect officers, approve the bank account, adopt the conflict-of-interest policy, and set the next meeting date. Add "Apply for EIN on irs.gov (free)" to your plan with a date after your articles are filed.
You can now get an EIN safely and for free, and run a first board meeting with the right decisions on the agenda.

check.q: What do you need an EIN for?
options: A bank account, payroll and tax-exemption applications
check.why: The EIN is the nonprofit's federal tax ID for banking, payroll and exemption applications.

check.q: You are filling in the IRS online EIN tool and need to stop halfway. What should you know?
options: You can save and finish next week
It must be finished in one sitting
AI can finish it for you
You can email the rest to the IRS
check.why: The IRS online tool must be finished in one sitting.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Tax exemption, registration and costs

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Applying for federal 501(c)(3) status
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose between Form 1023 and Form 1023-EZ and know the fee.
This lesson builds toward: Using the IRS eligibility worksheet, you will choose between Form 1023 and Form 1023-EZ and state where it is filed, with the fee taken from the official page.
To be a 501(c)(3) charity, most organizations apply to the IRS. There are two forms. Form 1023 is the full application; its user fee was $600 when we checked. Form 1023-EZ is a shorter form for small organizations; its fee was $275. Both are filed online on Pay.gov, and the fee is paid there when you file.
Not everyone can use the 1023-EZ. The IRS has an eligibility worksheet at the end of the Form 1023-EZ instructions. It looks at things like how much money you expect to raise and your assets. Fill in the worksheet honestly before you choose.
Churches have special rules: the IRS treats churches differently from other charities, and many are not required to apply, though some choose to. Read IRS Publication 1828 or ask a professional. When the IRS approves you, it sends a determination letter. Keep it forever: donors, grant makers and the state will ask for it.
Step by step:
- Open the Form 1023-EZ instructions on irs.gov and complete the eligibility worksheet.
- If you qualify and it fits, plan for the 1023-EZ; if not, plan for Form 1023.
- Create a Pay.gov account and complete the form there.
- Pay the user fee shown on the IRS user-fee page.
- Save the determination letter when it arrives.
Words to know:
- Form 1023: the full IRS application for 501(c)(3) status.
- Form 1023-EZ: the short IRS application for small organizations that pass the eligibility worksheet.
- User fee: the fee the IRS charges to review the application.
- Determination letter: the IRS letter that says your organization is tax-exempt.
Official sources:
- IRS: Form 1023 and 1023-EZ amount of user fee
- IRS: About Form 1023
- IRS: About Form 1023-EZ (eligibility worksheet is in the instructions)
- IRS Publication 1828: Tax Guide for Churches and Religious Organizations
Try it now: Open the Form 1023-EZ instructions on irs.gov and read the eligibility worksheet. Decide which form your nonprofit would file, then add that form, the fee from the IRS user-fee page, and a target date to your plan.
You can now decide between Form 1023 and 1023-EZ, find the current fee, and know where to file.

check.q: When is the IRS user fee for Form 1023 or 1023-EZ paid?
options: By check to the Secretary of State
check.why: Both forms are filed online on Pay.gov, and the fee is paid there when you file.

check.q: The IRS sends your determination letter. What do you do with it?
options: Throw it away after a year
Give the only copy to a donor
Keep it forever, because donors, grant makers and the state will ask for it
check.why: Keep the determination letter forever; many will ask for it.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: California exemption and the Registry of Charities
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan the Franchise Tax Board exemption and the Attorney General registration.
This lesson builds toward: After federal approval or your first donation, you will plan the Franchise Tax Board exemption and the Attorney General Registry registration, with the right form and the 30-day Registry deadline.
Federal approval does not make you exempt from California tax by itself. You also apply to the Franchise Tax Board (FTB). Form 3500 is the full California application. Form 3500A is a shorter form for organizations that already have their IRS determination letter. Check ftb.ca.gov for the current form, instructions and any fee before you file, because we could not confirm the fee on the FTB page for this course.
Charities that hold or raise money for charitable purposes in California also register with the Attorney General's Registry of Charities. You register online with Form CT-1 within 30 days of first receiving charitable assets, such as your first donation. The fee was $50 when we checked. You upload your articles, bylaws, IRS determination letter (or your EIN if you do not have it yet) and your Form 1023 or 1023-EZ if you filed one.
Some groups may be exempt from Registry registration. If you think yours is one (for example, a religious organization), read the Registry's pages or ask the Registry before you skip it.
Step by step:
- After the IRS letter arrives, plan Form 3500A on ftb.ca.gov (or Form 3500 if you apply without it).
- Note the date you first receive a donation or other charitable asset.
- Within 30 days of that date, register online with Form CT-1.
- Upload articles, bylaws, IRS letter or EIN, and your 1023 or 1023-EZ.
- Pay the Registry fee shown on oag.ca.gov.
Words to know:
- Franchise Tax Board (FTB): California's state tax agency.
- Form 3500A: the short California exemption form for groups that already have a federal 501(c)(3) letter.
- Registry of Charities: the Attorney General office that registers and oversees charities in California.
- CT-1: the Attorney General's initial registration form for charities.
Official sources:
- California Franchise Tax Board: Charities and nonprofits (Form 3500 / 3500A)
- California Attorney General: Registry of Charities, initial registration (CT-1)
Try it now: Add two rows to your plan: the FTB exemption (form name, "check fee on ftb.ca.gov", target date after the IRS letter) and the Attorney General CT-1 ($50, due within 30 days of your first donation). Make a list of the four documents you will upload.
You can now plan your California tax exemption and your Registry of Charities registration with the right forms, timing and documents.

check.q: Which form is the full California exemption application?
check.why: Form 3500 is the full California application; 3500A is the shorter one.

check.q: Your ministry thinks it may be exempt from Registry registration. What do you do?
options: Read the Registry's pages or ask the Registry before you skip it
check.why: Check the Registry's pages or ask the Registry before skipping registration.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Staying in good standing and your setup budget
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a start-up budget and a yearly filing calendar.
This lesson builds toward: Given the checked fees and due dates, you will build a start-up budget and a yearly filing calendar, with every fee and due date checked on the official page.
Starting is not the end. Every year you file with the IRS: small groups with gross receipts normally $50,000 or less can usually file the Form 990-N e-Postcard; larger ones file Form 990-EZ or 990. If you miss three years in a row, the IRS automatically takes away your tax-exempt status.
Every year you also renew with the Attorney General on Form RRF-1. The fee depends on total revenue: when we checked it was $25 under $50,000, $50 from $50,000 to $100,000, and $75 from $100,001 to $250,000, rising for larger charities. It is due 4 months and 15 days after your fiscal year ends (May 15 for a year ending December 31). You also have the Statement of Information every two years, and California annual filings with the FTB: check ftb.ca.gov for which form fits you.
Start-up government fees, as checked: articles $30, Statement of Information $20, EIN free, IRS $275 (1023-EZ) or $600 (1023), Registry $50, plus any FTB fee. That is about $375 with the 1023-EZ or $700 with Form 1023, before any FTB fee, a registered agent service, or a lawyer. Use AI to help draft a budget table or a reminder list, but check every number on the official page.
Step by step:
- List each start-up fee from the official pages.
- Add them up for your form choice (1023-EZ or 1023).
- Add yearly filings: IRS 990 series, Attorney General RRF-1, FTB annual filing.
- Add the Statement of Information every two years.
- Put every due date in a shared calendar with two reminders.
Words to know:
- Form 990-N: the IRS e-Postcard: a short yearly online notice for small exempt groups.
- RRF-1: the Attorney General's yearly renewal form for charities.
- Fiscal year: the 12-month period your nonprofit uses for its books, often January to December.
- Good standing: being up to date on all required filings and fees.
Official sources:
- IRS: Form 990-N (e-Postcard) for small exempt organizations
- California Attorney General: Registry of Charities, annual renewal (RRF-1)
- California Secretary of State: Statement of Information (SI-100 for nonprofits)
- IRS: Form 1023 and 1023-EZ amount of user fee
- California Secretary of State: Corporations - California (Domestic) forms and fees
- California Attorney General: Registry of Charities, initial registration (CT-1)
- California Franchise Tax Board: Charities and nonprofits (Form 3500 / 3500A)
Try it now: Final task: finish your one-page setup plan. Make a table with each filing in order, the office, the form, the fee from the official page, and your target date. Add the yearly filings and due dates, the total start-up cost, and the official link for each row.
You can now build a complete California nonprofit setup plan with costs and a yearly calendar that keeps the organization in good standing.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Filings in order A filing is missing or out of order. Every setup filing listed in the right order with its office. Notes why the order matters for at least two steps. Right forms A wrong form is named, such as mutual benefit articles for a charity. Each filing names the right form, including articles, SI-100, 1023 or 1023-EZ, 3500 or 3500A, and CT-1. Explains the choice between 1023 and 1023-EZ using the eligibility worksheet. Official fees and links A fee is guessed or has no link. Every fee comes from the official page, with a link, and the start-up total is added up. Notes the date each fee was checked. Planned dates No planned filing dates, or the 30-day Registry and 90-day SI-100 deadlines are missed. A planned date for each filing that meets every deadline. Names who on the board is responsible for each filing. Yearly calendar Yearly filings are missing. IRS yearly filing, RRF-1, the two-year Statement of Information and FTB filings, with due dates. Due dates are set as calendar reminders for the board. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which yearly filing goes to the Attorney General?
check.why: Every year you renew with the Attorney General on Form RRF-1.

check.q: AI drafts your start-up budget table. What do you do with the fees in it?
options: Trust them; AI is up to date
Check every number on the official page
check.why: Use AI to draft the table, but check every number on the official page.
